extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of journalism and mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate how individual-level factors (demographics, values, beliefs, experience, personality, outside activities) influence news selection, framing, and newsroom practice. Used for research, teaching, or newsroom policy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of journalists' demographics on news values and content (gender, race, sexual orientation, etc.) — described as an empirical question; Weaver and Wilhoit suggest the effect is probably minor given organizational routines and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that organizational routines may negate most individual differences; examples given include Farley (1978) finding female magazine publishers gave more favorable coverage to the ERA, and Goodrick (1991) showing female editorialists do not respond uniformly to 'women's issues.' Researchers should treat demographic influence as testable rather than assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in newsroom interactions from increased diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing numbers of women, minorities, and homosexuals in the newsroom can change interpersonal dynamics (e.g., reduction of sexist jokes, more collaborative meetings) but do not eliminate gender politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Marion Tuttle Marzolf interviewees and Stein (1993) reporting 'Cheesecake has virtually disappeared' and 'News meetings are a bit less confrontational.' Also counterexamples: panelists reported 'gender politics of the unwelcome kind' still pervade some newsrooms; anecdote of racial sexual remark leading to lawsuit and settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of beats based on reporter identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices and questions about whether reporters should be assigned stories based on their gender, race, or sexual orientation (e.g., 'Should women be allowed to cover abortion?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spike Lee requested African-American journalists to interview him about Malcolm X; LA Times refused citing policy that interviewees cannot select interviewers. The entry highlights tensions between giving opportunities to minority reporters and newsroom policies of impartial assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-bind and valuation of minority reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Minority journalists often face a double-bind: being assigned primarily to minority stories while being denied lead or directing roles on those stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1992 Los Angeles riots — minority reporters were assigned because of ethnicity but felt stories were undervalued and were not permitted to write lead stories or direct coverage. Quoted feelings of living in 'two worlds' (reporting objectively while feeling the community's rage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of reporters' sexual orientation on coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Gay and lesbian reporters may identify stories omitted by heterosexual colleagues, flag misleading language, and improve coverage of LGBTQ issues; absence of such reporters can lead to neglect (e.g., AIDS coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jeffrey Schmalz argued many gay stories are left out unless a gay reporter 'says there's a story there'; Randy Shilts argued lack of openly gay reporters harmed AIDS coverage. Study of senior editors found editors interested but ignorant about gay/lesbian issues and sometimes conflated AIDS coverage with community coverage (Brent & Greenwald).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy versus objectivity (group loyalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether journalists who are women, minorities, or homosexuals should advocate for their groups or adhere strictly to traditional journalistic objectivity; questions about 'ethnic loyalty versus the pursuit of truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes: Lincoln Millstein urging caution against becoming an advocacy group; Lovell Beaulieu describing the difficulty of criticizing members of one's racial group without communal backlash. The text contrasts traditional objectivity with arguments that explicit disclosure of viewpoint may be better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter background/expertise alignment with beat
rubrics_metrics.description: When demography relates to expertise (e.g., hiring local/foreign journalists or bilingual/bicultural reporters), coverage accuracy and sensitivity may improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scott Shuster advocating hiring local foreign journalists rather than 'parachuting' U.S. reporters; David Lawrence, Jr. advocating hiring U.S. Hispanics for bilingual/bicultural advantages. Counterexample: recruited Hispanics from outside local communities failed to identify local priorities (Greenberg et al., 1983).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selection and journalist personality type
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalism profession is self-selected and may attract a particular personality type (e.g., liking excitement, disliking abstractions), which affects beat choices and news preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hess (1981) suggests journalists prefer excitement and thus favor beats (Senate over House, politics over management) that provide it; personality research may explain why news is as it is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic personal values and belief systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists commonly hold a cluster of values (Gans' 'motherhood' values and Progressive-era values) such as ethnocentrism, altruistic democracy, responsible capitalism, small-town pastoralism, individualism, moderatism, social order, and leadership that shape news selection and description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each value affects story topics and framing (e.g., altruistic democracy underlies stories about public interest, small-town pastoralism produces nostalgic rural portrayals, individualism creates 'rugged individualist' hero narratives). The values are often implicit and found 'between the lines' of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal political attitudes (liberalism/conservatism and elite status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' political orientations (tendency toward Democratic identification among journalists and especially among 'elite' media) may influence news judgment and commentary; elites may differ from the average journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited studies: Lichter, Rothman, & Lichter's elite-study (high liberal percentage among elites) and Weaver & Wilhoit's probability sample (journalists slightly more likely to be Democrats than general population). The text notes debates over how much these attitudes affect reporting and whether elite journalists influence broader media agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal political activity and newsroom conflict-of-interest policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' outside partisan or civic activities can be restricted by employers to protect credibility; organizations may limit visible political involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Sandy Nelson removed from beat for organizing a referendum and told to forego political activity to return; Washington Post policy quoted: 'We avoid active involvement in any partisan causes...that could compromise or seem to compromise our ability to report and edit fairly.' Employers require disclosure of business or family ties that could appear to compromise integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal religious orientations and religion coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' religious affiliations (or secularism) and lack of religion beats can lead to uneven or uncritical coverage of religious news and susceptibility to blindspots or stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: elite journalists more secular; Weaver & Wilhoit show journalists' religious affiliations largely match society. Examples: fewer than 50 full-time religion editors among ~1,600 newspapers; analysis showing only half of 40 religious stories presented skeptical sources; ombudsman criticisms of blindspots and stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for bias ('bias that counts must be in the copy')
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction that personal attitudes alone are insufficient evidence of bias — the bias must be manifest in news content ('in the copy') rather than only in journalists' minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Robinson (1983): critics should look for bias in actual coverage. This sets a methodological standard for research or critique: demonstrate content-level bias rather than inferring it solely from reporters' attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldviews shaping news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' broader worldviews influence choices about sources, news pegs, and language; news judgment is subjective and reflects perceptions of social reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lichter: 'news judgment is subjective and decisions about sources, news pegs, and . . . language will partly reflect the way a journalist perceives and understands the social world.' Researchers should consider worldview as a mediating factor, distinct from discrete attitude measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational constraints vs individual attitudes and media convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational routines, professional norms, and institutional constraints often limit individual-level influences, but elite media can set agendas leading to convergence across outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaver & Wilhoit argue organizational constraints may negate individual differences; counterpoint: Reese & Danielian show convergence (e.g., cocaine coverage where New York Times set agenda for networks). Evaluations should weigh organizational factors and potential amplification by elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political correctness, censorship concerns, and editorial decision dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about 'political correctness' or censorship can shape editorial choices and debates about whether content is being suppressed or corrected for bias; these dynamics may obscure links between values and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mike Royko column initially killed as racist then ran after pushback; the text warns that labeling actions 'political correctness' shifts focus from values' influence to debates about censorship, complicating assessments of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence and methods for detecting attitude–coverage links
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies produce conflicting results; some show correlations between journalists' attitudes and how groups are covered, others document prejudice affecting descriptions — indicating the need for careful empirical design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Shoemaker (1984) correlated New York Times coverage legitimacy of groups with journalists' attitudes; Rainville & McCormick (1977) showed racial prejudice can influence communication. Guidance: use content analysis linked to reporter attitude data to test influence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/professional bias in local civic development coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' personal attachment to local civic development (e.g., pride in hometown downtown projects) can lead to uncritical, positively slanted initial coverage of redevelopment initiatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaniss (1991) example: reporters who live/work downtown may readily accept officials' claims about development benefits and ignore displacement or alternative fund uses. Analysts should examine reporters' residence/status and newsroom-symbolic needs when assessing coverage slant.
